newsitem.title: CANADA: BOC head says no central bank likes weak currency.
newsitem.headline: BOC head says no central bank likes weak currency.

text.p: Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen said on Wednesday that no central bank liked to have a weak currency because it indicated weakness in the underlying economy.
"I don't think any central bank ever likes to see a weak currency because it I think it typically is a sign of an economy that is not as strong as it should be," Thiessen told a news conference.

The head of Canada's central bank also said that economic fundamentals point to an upward trend in the Canadian dollar, and that the bank's recent "made in Canada" interest rate policy doesn't mean Canadian rates are totally independent of rate movements in other countries.

"The made-in-Canada monetary policy does not mean completely independent interest rates. Interest rates are always going to be affected by what goes on in the rest of the world. The crucial thing is to have a monetary policy where monetary conditions are appropriate over time in bringing about non-inflationary, and therefore sustainable growth," said Thiessen.

Thiessen said stronger economic growth in recent months has likely narrowed the country's output gap, which was last measured at 3.0 percent by the bank in November. When asked when Canada might reach full capacity, Thiessen said it could happen in the next couple of years but declined to be more specific.
When asked about plans for the Bank of Canada's 1.0-3.0 percent target range for inflation which expires in 1998, Thiessen said the central bank will review the target.

"We will decide what the targets are after that, but I guess as far as I'm concerned, the targets are to keep inflation low in Canada forever. That's the way you get good economic performance. That's the great lesson that we learned in the 1970's and '80's," said Thiessen.

Thiessen was also asked if the central bank was under pressure to keep interest rates on hold because of an expected Federal election in June. While he did not address the question directly, Thiessen reiterated that the Bank of Canada is an independent institution.

"The reason for establishing an independent central bank is so that monetary policy can be made in a forward looking context and without concern of political influence. That's what the central bank is there to do," said Thiessen.

Thiessen also said that the Bank of Canada remains focused on a broad number of indicators, including the monetary conditions index as well as other monetary aggregates, to judge the level of overall monetary conditions.
